claim: A regenerative response in the appendages of moon jellyfish, fruit flies, and mice can be promoted by nutrient modulation.
source: Previously we reported evidence that a regenerative response in the appendages of moon jellyfish, fruit flies, and mice can be promoted by nutrient modulation (Abrams et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abrams et al., 2021

claim: Sustar and Tuthill were unable to reproduce the induced regenerative response in flies.
source: Sustar and Tuthill subsequently reported that they had not been able to reproduce the induced regenerative response in flies (Sustar and Tuthill, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sustar and Tuthill, 2023

claim: Differences in amputation method, treatment concentrations, age of animals, and stress management explain why Sustar and Tuthill did not observe a regenerative response in flies.
source: Here we discuss that differences in the amputation method, treatment concentrations, age of the animals, and stress management explain why they did not observe a regenerative response in flies.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of protocols and experimental outcomes

claim: Typically, 30–50% of treated flies showed response in the authors' assay.
source: Typically, 30–50% of treated flies showed response in our assay.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the authors' protocol

claim: In adult frogs, limb regeneration can be induced by salt treatment, electrical stimulation, progenitor cell implantation, and drug cocktails.
source: In adult frogs, studies dating back to early 1900s (Carlson, 2007) demonstrate that limb regeneration can be induced by salt treatment, electrical stimulation, and in more recent studies, progenitor cell implantation (Lin et al., 2013) and drug cocktails (Murugan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carlson, 2007; Lin et al., 2013; and Murugan et al., 2022

claim: In fish, cardiomyocyte proliferation in the medaka can be induced by acute inflammation.
source: In fish, cardiomyocyte proliferation in the medaka can be induced by acute inflammation (Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2017

claim: In adult mice, a regenerative response can be promoted in multiple organs, including the heart, retinal axon, and limbs.
source: Even in adult mice, a regenerative response can be promoted in multiple organs, including the heart (Sadek and Olson, 2020), retinal axon (Bei et al., 2016), and limbs (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sadek and Olson, 2020; Bei et al., 2016; and Yu et al., 2012

claim: Adult Drosophila limb can be promoted to show regrowth by administering insulin and amino acids.
source: Adding to this body of work, we presented evidence that adult Drosophila limb can be promoted to show regrowth by administering insulin and amino acids (Abrams et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abrams et al., 2021

claim: Adult animals retain a capacity to mount a regenerative response greater than they normally show.
source: Although none of the induced regeneration is complete, these studies demonstrate the biological phenomenon that, in multiple species, adult animals retain a capacity to mount a regenerative response greater than they normally show.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple cited studies across species

claim: Amputation method is a key parameter that can profoundly alter the outcomes of regeneration processes.
source: Amputation method is a key parameter that can profoundly alter the outcomes of regeneration processes.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about regeneration experiments

claim: In studies of muscle repair in mice, injury models vary from surgically resecting a portion of the muscle, to applying pressure using heavy weight, to using a cold needle to kill muscle fibers, to applying toxins or chemicals.
source: For instance, in studies of muscle repair in mice, injury models vary from surgically resecting a portion of the muscle, to applying pressure using heavy weight, to using a cold needle to kill muscle fibers, to applying toxins or chemicals (Hardy et al., 2016; Sicherer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hardy et al., 2016 and Sicherer et al., 2020

claim: The way one introduces injury affects how the muscle is damaged, how much the surrounding cells and tissues are affected and, consequently, the molecular and tissue responses.
source: The way one introduces injury affects how the muscle is damaged, how much the surrounding cells and tissues are affected and, consequently, the molecular and tissue responses.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about injury models

claim: In highly regenerating animal models, the way one inflicts injury influences the extent of regeneration.
source: Even in highly regenerating animal models, the way one inflicts injury influences the extent of regeneration (e.g., in axolotl, see Kragl and Tanaka, 2009; in zebrafish, see Dickover et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kragl and Tanaka, 2009 and Dickover et al., 2013

claim: Sustar and Tuthill used a razor blade (American Safety Razor 72–003) to do their amputation.
source: Sustar and Tuthill used a razor blade to do their amputation (American Safety Razor 72–003).
evidence: Based on description of Sustar and Tuthill's methods

claim: The authors use Vannas surgical scissors (Fine Science Tools 91500–009) for amputation.
source: By contrast, as specified in our protocol, we use Vannas surgical scissors (Fine Science Tools 91500–009).
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol

claim: To do a cut with a razor blade, one has to press against the fly leg, thus introducing a different kind of injury.
source: To do a cut with a razor blade, one has to press against the fly leg, thus introducing a different kind of injury.
evidence: Based on inference about the mechanical requirements of using a razor blade

claim: In the authors' protocol, the muscle in the residual tibias typically remains largely in place immediately after amputation.
source: Figures 1a and 2 show how, in our protocol, the muscle in the residual tibias typically looks immediately after amputation. The residual muscle bundles recede a little from the amputation plane and have visibly lost some tension due to the amputation, but they remain largely in place.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1a and 2

claim: In the work of Sustar and Tuthill, the residual muscle bundles in the freshly amputated tibia collapse.
source: By contrast, in the work of Sustar and Tuthill (their Figure 2B), the residual muscle bundles in the freshly amputated tibia collapse (see illustrations in Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on observation of Sustar and Tuthill's Figure 2B and illustrated in the authors' Figure 1a

claim: The authors' protocol specifies flies aged between 2 and 7 days old for the amputation, with 3–5 day-olds being the most typical age.
source: Our protocol specifies flies aged between 2 and 7 days old for the amputation, with 3–5 day-olds being the most typical age we use.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol

claim: Sustar and Tuthill used 1–2 day old flies.
source: Sustar and Tuthill used 1–2 day old flies, because "young flies are more likely to regenerate and more likely to survive the three-week recovery period than old flies".
evidence: Based on description of Sustar and Tuthill's methods

claim: The authors deliberately avoided using 1-day-old flies because the cuticle is still maturing and extensive tissue remodeling still continues in newly eclosed flies.
source: We deliberately avoided using 1-day-old flies because the cuticle is still maturing and extensive tissue remodeling still continues in newly eclosed flies (Kimura and Truman, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kimura and Truman, 1990

claim: The mortality rate in the experiment of Sustar and Tuthill is double the rate from the authors' protocol.
source: As discussed below, the mortality rate in the experiment of Sustar and Tuthill is double the rate from our protocol (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Sustar and Tuthill used at least three times higher concentrations of insulin and amino acids in their experiment.
source: Sustar and Tuthill used at least three times higher concentrations of insulin and amino acids in their experiment.
evidence: Based on comparison of treatment concentrations between protocols

claim: The correct concentrations were given in the figure legend of Abrams et al., 2021, but the concentrations listed in the Materials and methods section of the article were incorrect.
source: We take responsibility for this discrepancy: although the correct concentrations were given in the figure legend of Abrams et al., 2021, the concentrations listed in the Materials and methods section of the article were incorrect; we have now published a correction for this article (Abrams et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to correction article Abrams et al., 2023

claim: CO2 exposure is known to alter physiological and behavioral processes and is considered stressful, increasing hemolymph acidity and reducing heartbeat.
source: CO2 exposure, however, is known to alter physiological and behavioral processes and is considered stressful, increasing hemolymph acidity and reducing heartbeat (Nicolas and Sillans, 1989; Badre et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nicolas and Sillans, 1989 and Badre et al., 2005

claim: Stress can impact wound healing and tissue regeneration.
source: Stress can impact wound healing and tissue regeneration (Sallin and Jaźwińska, 2016; Hachemi et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2013; Christian et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sallin and Jaźwińska, 2016; Hachemi et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2013; and Christian et al., 2006

claim: Sustar and Tuthill anesthetized a large group of flies at a time (20 flies), and kept the anesthesia time 5 minutes.
source: Sustar and Tuthill anesthetized a large group of flies at a time (20 flies), and kept the anesthesia time 5 minutes.
evidence: Based on description of Sustar and Tuthill's methods

claim: The authors anesthetize fewer flies at a time (1–2 flies for the measurements), and keep the anesthesia time much shorter (1–3 minutes).
source: By contrast, we anesthetize fewer flies at a time (1–2 flies for the measurements), and keep the anesthesia time much shorter (1–3 minutes).
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol

claim: The authors use CO2 at a much lower flow rate (2–3 litres/min) than that typically used for regular housekeeping (~5–10 litres/min).
source: Moreover, we use CO2 at a much lower flow rate than that typically used for regular housekeeping. While housekeeping CO2 flow rate (~5–10 litres/min) usually puts flies to sleep almost immediately, we reduce CO2 flow to the lowest amount possible (2–3 litres/min), just enough to keep the flies from walking—a similar strategy used in other sensitive protocols (e.g., Landis et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol and citation to Landis et al., 2020

claim: Increasing the anesthesia time in the authors' protocol is enough to reduce the frequency of flies responding to the treatment.
source: Increasing the anesthesia time in our protocol is enough to reduce the frequency of flies responding to the treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: Housing density is a variable in fly study that can impact various physiological traits, and is a stressor.
source: Housing density is another variable in fly study that can impact various physiological traits, and is a stressor (Nath Das et al., 2022; Joshi and Mueller, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nath Das et al., 2022 and Joshi and Mueller, 1997

claim: The authors house ≤6 flies per vial.
source: As specified in our protocol, we house ≤6 flies per vial.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol

claim: Increasing the housing density in the authors' protocol is enough to reduce the frequency of flies responding to the treatment.
source: Increasing the housing density in our protocol is enough to reduce the frequency of flies responding to the treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: In the experiment of Sustar and Tuthill, 51% of the control fly amputees died by three weeks post amputation.
source: In the experiment of Sustar and Tuthill, 51% of the control fly amputees died by three weeks post amputation (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b, citing Sustar and Tuthill's results

claim: In the authors' experiment, 14% of the control flies died by three weeks post amputation.
source: By contrast, in our experiment, 14% of the control flies died by three weeks post amputation.
evidence: Supported by the authors' experimental data

claim: 49% of the treated flies showed a change in the residual limb length that is beyond the measurement noise.
source: As shown in the measurements to which they refer (Figure 5e in Abrams et al., 2021), 49% of the treated flies showed a change in the residual limb length that is beyond the measurement noise (the 95% confidence intervals of the measurements in control flies).
evidence: Supported by data from Figure 5e in Abrams et al., 2021

claim: Flies that showed limb growth also tend to show a modified wound healing response, apparent within three days after amputation, from the absence of scab formation over the wound.
source: Moreover, the flies that respond to the treatment can be readily identified by eye. Flies that showed limb growth also tend to show a modified wound healing response, apparent within three days after amputation, from the absence of scab formation over the wound.
evidence: Supported by the authors' experimental observations

claim: Scab formation is a genetically controlled process linked to immune signaling.
source: This is a non-trivial phenotype, as scab formation is a genetically controlled process linked to immune signaling (Galko and Krasnow, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Galko and Krasnow, 2004

claim: The response to the treatment occurs in a significant fraction of flies (30–50%).
source: Therefore, the response to the treatment occurs in a significant fraction of flies (30–50%), manifests in processes occurring at multiple time scales after injury, and can be screened by eye from the modified wound healing.
evidence: Supported by the authors' experimental data

claim: In some regenerating systems, regeneration proceeds through the formation of a structure called blastema.
source: In some regenerating systems, regeneration proceeds through the formation of a structure called blastema.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about regeneration

claim: A blastema is usually composed of dedifferentiated cells that give rise to tissues to replace the lost structures.
source: A blastema is usually composed of dedifferentiated cells that give rise to tissues to replace the lost structures.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about blastema

claim: Blastema characterization was outside the scope of the authors' paper and they did not make any suggestions about a blastema structure.
source: However, blastema characterization was outside the scope of our paper and we did not make any suggestions about a blastema structure.
evidence: Statement about the scope of the authors' previous work

claim: Sustar and Tuthill analyzed a white blob phenotype that occurs in both control and treated flies at the same frequency (3–4%).
source: To assess a blastema formation, Sustar and Tuthill analyzed a white blob phenotype, that occurs in both control and treated flies, and both at the same frequency (3–4%).
evidence: Based on description of Sustar and Tuthill's analysis

claim: The authors do not observe in their protocol a phenotype that occurs in both control and treatment at equal frequency.
source: We do not observe in our protocol a phenotype that occurs in both control and treatment at equal frequency.
evidence: Supported by the authors' experimental observations

claim: The significant differences in the way Sustar and Tuthill performed the protocol led to serious differences in the nature of the injury and mortality rate, which can explain why they did not see a regenerative response.
source: In summary, the significant differences in the way Sustar and Tuthill performed the protocol led to serious differences in the nature of the injury and mortality rate, which can explain why they did not see a regenerative response.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of protocols and outcomes

claim: The authors have published a step-by-step detailed protocol of this work, along with highlights of the critical parameters.
source: However, the work of Sustar and Tuthill helped emphasize to us the sensitive parts of the protocol, so we have now published a step-by-step detailed protocol of this work, along with highlights of the critical parameters discussed here (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2023

claim: It is established that adult insects do not regenerate.
source: It is established that adult insects do not regenerate.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: Sustar and Tuthill argue that adult insects cannot regenerate because they lack the developmental mechanisms to support new growth, due to epigenetic silencing.
source: Sustar and Tuthill argue that adult insects cannot regenerate because they lack the developmental mechanisms to support new growth, due to epigenetic silencing (Harris et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on description of Sustar and Tuthill's argument with citations to Harris et al., 2020 and Fox et al., 2020

claim: Epigenetic silencing can be modulated.
source: However, the very study they cite (Harris et al., 2020) shows that epigenetic silencing can be modulated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2020

claim: Epigenetic regulations can be modulated by multiple factors including nutrients.
source: Indeed, multiple studies describe how epigenetic regulations can be modulated, by multiple factors including nutrients (Dai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dai et al., 2020

claim: Adult animals that do not normally regenerate retain the capacity to activate a regenerative response.
source: Our findings in Drosophila add to the increasing body of evidence in the regeneration field that adult animals that do not normally regenerate retain the capacity to activate a regenerative response.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple studies including the authors' work

claim: Relatively simple interventions can unlock regenerative capacity in adult animals.
source: As described in the introduction, what is emerging from work across multiple species is that relatively simple interventions can unlock this regenerative capacity, which speaks to us as to the nature of the biological regulations involved.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple studies across species

claim: Amputation was performed on adult flies 2–7 days after eclosion.
source: As described in Abrams et al., 2021 and detailed in Li et al., 2023, amputation was performed on adult flies 2–7 days after eclosion.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' methods with citations to Abrams et al., 2021 and Li et al., 2023

claim: After amputation, flies were reared with the lab food (control) or lab food supplemented with the leucine, insulin and glutamine mix.
source: After amputation, flies were reared with the lab food (control) or lab food supplemented with the leucine, insulin and glutamine mix.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' methods

claim: The treatment master mix contained 1.7 mM L-Leucine, 1.7 mM L-Glutamine, and 0.33 μg/ml insulin.
source: To make the treared vials, first we made an aqueous master mix of 1.7 mM L-Leucine (Sigma-Aldrich L8912), 1.7 mM L-Glutamine (Sigma-Aldrich G3126), and 0.33 μg/ml insulin (human recombinant, Sigma-Aldrich I0908).
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' methods

claim: Flies were kept in treatment for 4–5 days, and then moved to regular food.
source: Flies were kept in treatment for 4–5 days, and then moved to regular food.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' methods

claim: Freshly dissected limbs were imaged using the Zeiss LSM 980 laser-scanning confocal microscope, with 63x/1.4 Oil Plan-Apochromat objective.
source: For fluorescence imaging, freshly dissected limbs were imaged using the Zeiss LSM 980 laser-scanning confocal microscope, with 63x/1.4 Oil Plan-Apochromat objective.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' methods

claim: In the authors' amputation method, muscle bundles in the residual tibia remain in place.
source: In our amputation method, muscle bundles in the residual tibia remain in place (see Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: In the method used by Sustar and Tuthill, muscle bundles collapsed.
source: By contrast, in the method used by Sustar and Tuthil, muscle bundles collapsed (see their Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on observation of Sustar and Tuthill's Figure 2B

claim: The lack of stress management in the protocol of Sustar and Tuthill is reflected in the much higher mortality rate in their experiment.
source: The lack of stress management in the protocol of Sustar and Tuthill is reflected in the much higher mortality rate in their experiment (as reported in their Table 1).
evidence: Based on inference from mortality data in Sustar and Tuthill's Table 1

claim: Increasing the CO2 exposure time to five minutes is enough to halve the frequency of flies responding to the treatment.
source: Even at thissub-anesthetic CO2 level, increasing the CO2 exposure time to five minutes is enough to halving the frequency of flies responding to the treatment.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The authors normally place up to 6 flies per vial after amputation.
source: After amputation, we normally place up to 6 flies per vial.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The effects of the treatment were assessed three days after amputation by the absence of scab formation over the amputation site.
source: In these experiments, adult flies were amputated across the tibia, and placed on food supplemented with leucine, glutamine, and insulin. The effects of the treatment were assessed three days after amputation by the absence of scab formation over the amputation site.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental methods in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The authors analyzed Mhc-GFP flies, in which promoter of the muscle-specific myosin heavy chain (Mhc) gene drives GFP expression.
source: To assess the muscle structure in the limb, we analyzed the Mhc-GFP flies, in which promoter of the muscle-specific myosin heavy chain (Mhc) gene drives GFP expression.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental methods in Figure 2

claim: The residual muscle bundles recede a little from the amputation plane and have visibly lost some tension due to the amputation, but they remain largely in place.
source: The residual muscle bundles recede a little from the amputation plane and have visibly lost some tension due to the amputation, but they remain largely in place.
evidence: Supported by the authors' observations of muscle structure after amputation

claim: The cuticle is still maturing in 1-day-old flies.
source: We deliberately avoided using 1-day-old flies because the cuticle is still maturing and extensive tissue remodeling still continues in newly eclosed flies (Kimura and Truman, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kimura and Truman, 1990

claim: Extensive tissue remodeling still continues in newly eclosed flies.
source: We deliberately avoided using 1-day-old flies because the cuticle is still maturing and extensive tissue remodeling still continues in newly eclosed flies (Kimura and Truman, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kimura and Truman, 1990

claim: The authors anesthetize flies using the lowest possible CO2 level, and limit anesthesia duration to one to three minutes.
source: To perform the amputation, we normally anesthetize the flies using the lowest possible CO2 level, and limit anesthesia duration to one to three minutes.
evidence: Supported by description of the authors' protocol in Figure 1—figure supplement 1
